scenes.visual: Title card 'Putting the Switch on Trial' on the same pale sea-green background as the first film. SAME COLOUR MAP as the first film: marine fish and marine DNA BLUE; Paxton Lake fish and Paxton DNA ORANGE; Pitx1 RNA GOLD; DNA a charcoal ribbon; enhancers are rectangular switch tabs on the DNA. New in this film: the reporter glow is GREEN. The pelvis is a small bony girdle on the belly with a pair of long spines. Flat side-view cartoons only.

scenes.tts: The hybrid test pinned the fault on the lake copy's own DNA. Pit ex one RNA is missing where the pelvis forms. So which stretch of DNA is the broken pelvic switch? And how would you prove it? The colours are the same: blue for marine, orange for Paxton, gold for Pit ex one RNA.
scenes.caption: The hybrid test pinned the fault on the lake copy's own DNA. Pitx1 RNA is missing where the pelvis forms. So which stretch of DNA is the broken pelvic switch? And how would you prove it? The colours are the same: blue for marine, orange for Paxton, gold for Pitx1 RNA.
scenes.visual: Open on two DNA copies side by side in one cell nucleus, one BLUE and one ORANGE; the ORANGE copy gets a small red flag labelled 'fault on this copy (pelvis)'. Then the ORANGE Paxton larva with GOLD only in the jaw and an empty dashed circle on the belly; a question mark appears over the belly. A colour key slides in at the bottom: BLUE 'marine', ORANGE 'Paxton', GOLD 'Pitx1 RNA'.
scenes.narration: The hybrid test pinned the fault on the lake copy's own DNA. Pitx1 RNA is missing where the pelvis forms. So which stretch of DNA is the broken pelvic switch? And how would you prove it? The colours are the same: blue for marine, orange for Paxton, gold for Pitx1 RNA.

scenes.tts: Here is the suspect, a stretch of noncoding DNA just upstream of the gene. It was first called Pell. A second switch was found later, so this one became Pell A. Three tests put it on trial.
scenes.caption: Here is the suspect, a stretch of noncoding DNA just upstream of the gene. It was first called Pel. A second switch was found later, so this one became PelA. Three tests put it on trial.
scenes.visual: Zoom along the charcoal DNA ribbon to the region in front of the Pitx1 coding block. A switch tab there is circled with a magnifying glass and labelled 'PelA (upstream enhancer)'. A courtroom-style label slides in: 'Suspect: PelA'.
scenes.narration: Here is the suspect, a stretch of noncoding DNA just upstream of the gene. It was first called Pel. A second switch was found later, so this one became PelA. Three tests put it on trial.

scenes.tts: First test: a reporter. Cut out the suspect DNA. Join it to a short start signal and a gene for a visible marker. Put that into fish embryos, and watch where the marker turns on.
scenes.visual: Scissors cut the PelA tab out of the ribbon. It is snapped onto a short block labelled 'minimal promoter' and a block labelled 'marker gene (glows GREEN)'. The finished construct, labelled 'reporter', is injected by a fine needle into a cartoon fish embryo.
scenes.narration: First test: a reporter. Cut out the suspect DNA. Join it to a short start signal and a gene for a visible marker. Put that into fish embryos, and watch where the marker turns on.

scenes.tts: The marine version of Pell A drove the marker in the developing pelvis. The Paxton version carries a deletion. It gave pelvic expression in none of the fish tested, as the counter shows.
scenes.caption: The marine version of PelA drove the marker in the developing pelvis. The Paxton version carries a deletion. It gave pelvic expression in none of the fish tested, as the counter shows.
scenes.visual: Two larvae side by side. Left, labelled 'marine PelA reporter', BLUE outline: a GREEN glow appears on the belly where the pelvis forms. Right, labelled 'Paxton PelA reporter', ORANGE outline: the ORANGE PelA tab above it has a visible gap, labelled 'deletion'; its belly stays dark. A counter under the right larva reads '0 of 8 fish with pelvic expression'.
scenes.narration: The marine version of PelA drove the marker in the developing pelvis. The Paxton version carries a deletion. It gave pelvic expression in none of the fish tested, as the counter shows.

scenes.tts: So the Paxton switch drives no pelvic glow. Does that prove the fish's own pelvis needs Pell A?
scenes.caption: So the Paxton switch drives no pelvic glow. Does that prove the fish's own pelvis needs PelA?
scenes.visual: The dark ORANGE larva holds centre screen. On-screen text: 'No glow. Does the pelvis need PelA?' with two buttons, 'yes' and 'not yet'.
scenes.narration: So the Paxton switch drives no pelvic glow. Does that prove the fish's own pelvis needs PelA?

scenes.visual: Hold the question. A small countdown ring fills over five seconds.

scenes.tts: Not yet. A reporter shows what a sequence can drive, inside a construct. It does not show that the body depends on it. For that, you change the fish itself.
scenes.visual: The 'not yet' button lights. The reporter construct floats out of the larva, labelled 'construct: what the sequence CAN drive'. Beside it a whole fish appears, labelled 'the body: does form DEPEND on it?'. An arrow points from the first label to the second, marked 'a different question'.
scenes.narration: Not yet. A reporter shows what a sequence can drive, inside a construct. It does not show that the body depends on it. For that, you change the fish itself.

scenes.tts: Each test answers its own question. A reporter asks what a sequence can drive. Adding the switch back asks whether that can restore form. Removing it from the animal asks whether form depends on it.
scenes.visual: A three-step ladder builds from the bottom up, one rung per sentence: rung 1 'reporter: what CAN it drive?' (GREEN glow icon), rung 2 'add it back: can it restore form?' (BLUE PelA tab plus a spine icon), rung 3 'remove it from the animal: does form DEPEND on it?' (a tab with a gap at its native place on the DNA).
scenes.narration: Each test answers its own question. A reporter asks what a sequence can drive. Adding the switch back asks whether that can restore form. Removing it from the animal asks whether form depends on it.

scenes.tts: Rescue comes closer. Marine Pell A, driving Pit ex one, was put into fertilized eggs from another pelvic-reduced lake. Those fish normally grow no pelvic spine. Compared with uninjected siblings, pelvic spine growth was variably enhanced.
scenes.caption: Rescue comes closer. Marine PelA, driving Pitx1, was put into fertilized eggs from another pelvic-reduced lake. Those fish normally grow no pelvic spine. Compared with uninjected siblings, pelvic spine growth was variably enhanced.
scenes.visual: A BLUE PelA tab clips onto a short Pitx1 block, labelled 'marine PelA + Pitx1'. A needle injects it into a row of ORANGE-tinted eggs, tagged 'Bear Paw Lake, Alaska (another pelvic-reduced population)'. The eggs hatch into two rows of juveniles: 'uninjected siblings' with no external pelvic spines (at most a tiny internal vestige), and 'injected' fish with variable spine development, some with clear external spines, others with little or none. A tag reads 'variable'. Schematic, not measured lengths.
scenes.narration: Rescue comes closer. Marine PelA, driving Pitx1, was put into fertilized eggs from another pelvic-reduced lake. Those fish normally grow no pelvic spine. Compared with uninjected siblings, pelvic spine growth was variably enhanced.

scenes.tts: Now the wild fish. Many pelvic-reduced populations carry deletions at Pell A. The deletions differ in where they start and stop. So the same switch was lost more than once.
scenes.caption: Now the wild fish. Many pelvic-reduced populations carry deletions at PelA. The deletions differ in where they start and stop. So the same switch was lost more than once.
scenes.visual: A schematic map of northern coasts and lakes (labelled 'schematic'). Lake pins pop up one by one. Beside each, an ORANGE PelA bar appears with a gap cut out; the gaps sit at different positions and lengths, all overlapping the middle of the bar. A vertical dashed line through the overlapping part is labelled 'same switch'.
scenes.narration: Now the wild fish. Many pelvic-reduced populations carry deletions at PelA. The deletions differ in where they start and stop. So the same switch was lost more than once.

scenes.tts: In one survey, deletions turned up in most pelvic-reduced populations, as the tally shows. None of the pelvis-complete populations had them. Common, then, but not universal. Most of the others showed signs of another route.
scenes.visual: A two-row tally board builds beneath the map. Row 1, 'pelvic-reduced populations': 13 ORANGE fish icons, 9 of them marked with a gap symbol, counter '9 of 13'. Row 2, 'pelvis-complete populations': 21 BLUE fish icons, none marked, counter '0 of 21'. The 4 unmarked reduced icons get a small tag 'other routes?'.
scenes.narration: In one survey, deletions turned up in most pelvic-reduced populations, as the tally shows. None of the pelvis-complete populations had them. Common, then, but not universal. Most of the others showed signs of another route.

scenes.tts: Different deletions, same switch. Pelvic reduction evolved again and again by losing one enhancer, in many lakes but not all. The deletions hit the switch, not the Pit ex one protein.
scenes.visual: The map's lake pins all link with thin lines to one ORANGE PelA tab, which flips flat. The BLUE marine fish and an ORANGE lake fish sit below: the BLUE pelvis bright, the ORANGE belly bare, GOLD still in both jaws.
scenes.caption: Different deletions, same switch. Pelvic reduction evolved again and again by losing one enhancer, in many lakes but not all. The deletions hit the switch, not the Pitx1 protein.
scenes.narration: Different deletions, same switch. Pelvic reduction evolved again and again by losing one enhancer, in many lakes but not all. The deletions hit the switch, not the Pitx1 protein.

scenes.visual: End card with the logo hexagon. Line: 'In many lakes, pelvic loss evolved by deleting the same Pitx1 switch.'
